explanations.explanation: Careful, friend, this one flips it around. The LORD says, “Do not learn the ways of the nations or be terrified by the signs in the heavens…” The nations are the ones who get terrified by them. Israel is told not to join in.

Right, the LORD says the opposite. He says, “Do not learn the ways of the nations or be terrified by the signs in the heavens, though the nations themselves are terrified by them.” So the nations panic, and Israel is told not to. Nobody needs to copy the person screaming at the sky.

explanations.answer: A tree cut down from the forest
explanations.explanation: Yes, it starts with a tree cut down from the forest. Before any silver or gold shows up, it's just wood, and a craftsman shapes it with a chisel. Something that started out standing in the woods is about to get called a god. I need a minute with that.

explanations.answer: A stone dug up from the riverbed
explanations.explanation: Stone is a sensible guess, but the passage doesn't say that. It says they cut down a tree from the forest. Then a craftsman shapes it with a chisel. Wood is where this one begins.

explanations.answer: A lump of clay from the potter
explanations.explanation: Clay is a fair guess, friend, but nobody in this passage mentions a potter. The text says they cut down a tree from the forest. A craftsman then shapes it with a chisel. So the first ingredient is wood.
That's it. They fasten it with hammer and nails so that it will not totter. Silver and gold all over it, and it still needs help standing up. I'd love to hear the sales pitch for that one.
The text never mentions thieves. It gives one reason: so that it will not totter. The nails are keeping it upright, not keeping anybody out. Hammer, nails and a wobbly idol is the whole picture.

explanations.answer: So it faces the right way
explanations.explanation: Which way it faces isn't in the passage, friend. The text says they fasten it with hammer and nails so that it will not totter. The point is staying upright, nothing about direction. I'd say that's a pretty low bar for a god.
Carried is right. The passage says, “They must be carried because they cannot walk.” I get around my bakery by hopping, gold base and all. These idols can't even manage that.
Hidden is a fair guess, but the passage says something else. It says they cannot speak and cannot walk, so “They must be carried.” Nobody is tucking them away here. They just can't move themselves.

Rebuilding isn't mentioned here, friend. The passage says, “They must be carried because they cannot walk.” Walking is the problem, and carrying is the fix. Somebody has to haul them wherever they're going.

explanations.answer: They can do no harm and no good
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “Do not fear them, for they can do no harm, and neither can they do any good.” There's nothing to be afraid of, and nothing to hope for either. It's a scarecrow in a cucumber patch with a lot more jewelry.

explanations.answer: They are too far away to hurt anyone
explanations.explanation: Distance isn't the reason the text gives. The LORD says, “Do not fear them, for they can do no harm, and neither can they do any good.” The idols themselves are the problem, not how far away they are. They can't do harm up close either.

explanations.answer: The LORD has already broken them
explanations.explanation: The passage doesn't say He has broken them, friend. Here the reason is that they can do no harm, and neither can they do any good. Verse 11 does say these gods will perish, but that comes later. For this question the answer is what the idols can't do.
That's right. The passage says that among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their kingdoms, “there is none like You.” Not one of them comes close. You can search every kingdom you want.

Close, but the number is lower than that. The passage says, “there is none like You,” and that covers all the wise men of the nations and all their kingdoms. A few would still be a few too many. The count is zero.

Even the wisest one doesn't make the list. The passage says that among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their kingdoms, “there is none like You.” Nobody gets an exception here. Not even the guy with the biggest scroll collection.

Yes. The passage says, “Hammered silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz.” So the materials get shipped in from far and wide. That's a whole supply chain for something that can't walk to the door.

Damascus is a real place, friend, but this passage doesn't name it here. It says, “Hammered silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz.” The silver comes from Tarshish. Good guess on a place name, though.

Nineveh is a real place, but it isn't the answer here. The passage says, “Hammered silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz.” Tarshish is where the silver comes from. Hang on to Nineveh, though, in case it shows up somewhere else.

That's right. The passage says the idols' clothes are blue and purple, “all fashioned by skilled workers.” So it's a custom outfit, tailored just right. And the idol can't even hold still without nails.

Priests aren't mentioned in these verses. The passage says their clothes are blue and purple, “all fashioned by skilled workers.” The ones sewing are skilled workers. I think that's a lot of effort for something that won't thank them.
Royal servants don't show up here, friend. The passage says the clothes are blue and purple, “all fashioned by skilled workers.” That's who made the outfits. The text doesn't say who ordered them.
Yes, living. The passage says, “But the LORD is the true God; He is the living God and eternal King.” The idols have no breath in them, as verse 14 says. The LORD is alive, and He's King forever.

Silent describes the idols, not the LORD. Back in verse 5 the idols cannot speak. For the LORD, the passage says, “He is the living God and eternal King.” That's the difference the passage keeps pointing at.
Hidden isn't the word here, friend. The passage says, “He is the living God and eternal King.” The word is living. The idols are the ones that get carried around and nailed down.

explanations.answer: They will perish from this earth
explanations.explanation: That's it. The words say these gods “…will perish from this earth and from under these heavens.” They don't get to stay on a shelf forever. They're going away.

explanations.answer: They will be locked away in a temple
explanations.explanation: Locking them in a temple isn't what the words say. They say these gods “…will perish from this earth and from under these heavens.” So perishing is the outcome, not being stored somewhere. No lock on any door can fix that.

explanations.answer: They will be melted down into coins
explanations.explanation: Coins aren't in the passage, friend. The words say these gods “…will perish from this earth and from under these heavens.” That's the outcome the text gives. It never says what becomes of the gold.
Yes. The passage says, “When He thunders, the waters in the heavens roar.” It's the LORD's thunder, and the sky answers. Try getting that out of something held together with nails.

Lions would make a great roar, but they aren't in this verse. The passage says, “When He thunders, the waters in the heavens roar.” The roaring comes from the waters above. Nothing in the forest is part of it.
Mountains aren't mentioned in this verse, friend. It says, “When He thunders, the waters in the heavens roar.” So the sky is what's roaring. The waters in the heavens answer the thunder.
Hold on, friend, it says the opposite. The passage says, “…every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols.” Shame, not pride. The goldsmith ends up embarrassed by the very thing he made.
That's it. The passage says, “…every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols.” He's put to shame, not proud. Imagine hammering away for weeks and the thing makes you look foolish.
Fraud is right. The passage says, “For his molten images are a fraud, and there is no breath in them.” They look impressive, but nothing's behind it. All shine and no breath.
I see why you'd say treasure, with all that gold and silver. But the passage says the molten images are a fraud, and there is no breath in them. They look valuable and they aren't what they claim.

Blessing is a nice word, but it isn't what the text says. It says the molten images are a fraud, and there is no breath in them. A blessing has to come from somebody. These images have no breath at all.

explanations.answer: He is the Maker of all things
explanations.explanation: Yes. The passage says, “…He is the Maker of all things…” The idols had to be made by somebody, and the LORD made everything. That's the whole gap between them.
Temples aren't brought up in this verse, friend. The reason given is, “…He is the Maker of all things…” It isn't about size or buildings. It's about who made what.
Counting worshipers isn't the reason in this verse. The passage says, “…He is the Maker of all things…” That's the difference between Him and the idols. It has nothing to do with crowds.

That's right. The passage says, “…Israel is the tribe of His inheritance…” The LORD is called the Portion of Jacob, and Israel is His inheritance. It's a warm way to close out all that talk about idols.
This one's actually in the passage, friend. It says, “…Israel is the tribe of His inheritance…” So the statement is true. After all those idols, the passage ends on something the LORD holds dear.
